name: Video game music
description: Composers, sound hardware and soundtracks from games.
curatedFacts: The Legend of Zelda's overworld theme was written in a single day, after Ravel's "Boléro" turned out to still be under copyright.
The NES sound chip had five channels: two pulse waves, a triangle, a noise channel, and one for samples.
The Tetris theme most people know is "Korobeiniki," a 19th-century Russian folk song.
Nobuo Uematsu wrote the music for the first nine Final Fantasy games.
The SNES sound chip could play eight channels at once — a big leap over the NES's five.
Sonic the Hedgehog's soundtrack was composed by Masato Nakamura, bassist of the band Dreams Come True.
Chrono Trigger's score was a collaboration between Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu.
Minecraft's soundtrack was written by Daniel Rosenfeld, who releases music as C418.
Koji Kondo composed the Super Mario Bros. theme — one of the most recognized pieces of music ever written.
Halo's main theme opens with monastic-style chanting, an unusual choice for a sci-fi shooter.
Yoko Shimomura composed the music for Kingdom Hearts and, years earlier, Street Fighter II.
Undertale's soundtrack was written by the game's own creator, Toby Fox.
Celeste's score was composed by Lena Raine, who later wrote music for Minecraft.
Michiru Yamane's score for Castlevania: Symphony of the Night mixes baroque, jazz and rock.
The Game Boy had four sound channels: two pulse waves, a wavetable channel, and noise.
Katamari Damacy's soundtrack pulls in jazz, samba and J-pop, with a different guest vocalist on many tracks.
Nier: Automata's score by Keiichi Okabe is sung in an invented language built from several real ones.
Yuzo Koshiro wrote the Streets of Rage music to sound like the club dance records he was listening to.
Persona 5's soundtrack by Shoji Meguro runs on acid jazz — organ, wah guitar and a live vocalist.
Super Mario Galaxy was the first Mario platformer scored for a live orchestra.
Doom's 1993 soundtrack by Bobby Prince was written to sound like the metal bands the developers played in the office.
Ocarina of Time made the player perform the music: songs played on the ocarina change time, weather and place.
Grant Kirkhope's Banjo-Kazooie score shifts instruments as you move between areas, without ever stopping the tune.
Jun Ishikawa has scored the Kirby series since the very first game in 1992.
